title: Concurrency basics
scopeHtml: Scope: race conditions, critical sections, mutex, spinlock, semaphores, condition variables, atomics, memory ordering and spotting lock contention. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Race conditions
notes.html:
A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the exact timing of two threads. Two threads touch the same data, at least one writes, and nothing orders them. The program works 999,999 times and corrupts data on the millionth.

The classic: counter++ looks like one step but is three: load the value into a register, add 1, store it back. Two threads can both load 5, both add 1, both store 6. One increment is lost.

Thread A            Thread B            counter in memory
load  r1 = 5                            5
                    load  r2 = 5        5
add   r1 = 6                            5
                    add   r2 = 6        5
store counter = 6                       6
                    store counter = 6   6   <- should be 7

Worked example. Two threads each run counter++ 1,000,000 times with no protection. Expected 2,000,000. Typical result on a 4-core box: about 1.1 to 1.5 million, different every run. Under a debugger or with a printf added the bug often vanishes, because timing changes. That is the signature of a race: a "Heisenbug".

# Detect it: build with ThreadSanitizer and run
gcc -fsanitize=thread -g race.c -o race -lpthread && ./race
# WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race (pid=4121)
#   Write of size 4 at 0x... by thread T2:
#     #0 worker race.c:9
#   Previous write of size 4 at 0x... by thread T1:
#     #0 worker race.c:9

A data race (formal: unsynchronised conflicting accesses) is not the same as a race condition (a logic bug depending on ordering). You can have a race condition with no data race: two threads each take a lock correctly, but "check balance then withdraw" is done in two separate locked steps, so both pass the check.

Industry examples. The Therac-25 radiation overdoses (1980s) involved a race in the operator-input code. The 2003 US Northeast blackout was partly blamed on a race in an alarm system (GE XA/21). Java's HashMap used from many threads has been known to loop forever in get under concurrent resize (pre-Java 8). Go ships a built-in detector (go run -race) and many companies run it in CI.

Everyday analogy. Two people editing the same paper form at once: both read "seats left: 5", both write "4", and the airline sells 6 tickets for 5 seats.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing counter++ is atomic because it is one line of code. It is not, even in C, Java or Kotlin.
  • Confusing data race with race condition. Name both; give the check-then-act example for the second.
  • Saying "volatile fixes it". volatile gives visibility, not atomic read-modify-write.

notes.title: Critical sections
notes.html:
A critical section is the piece of code that touches shared data and must run by only one thread at a time. Everything else the thread does can run in parallel. The goal is to make critical sections as small as possible, because while one thread is inside, all others wait.

A correct solution to mutual exclusion needs three properties:

  1. Mutual exclusion: at most one thread inside.
  2. Progress: if the section is free and someone wants in, someone gets in; no deadlock from the protocol itself.
  3. Bounded waiting: no thread waits forever (no starvation).

Worked example. A request handler spends 50 microseconds parsing (parallel), then 5 microseconds updating a shared stats table (critical), then 200 microseconds writing the response (parallel). Only 5 of 255 microseconds are serialised. By Amdahl's law, the maximum speed-up is 1 / serial fraction = 255 / 5 = 51x. If you wrongly hold the lock during the response write, the serial part is 205 of 255, and the cap drops to about 1.2x. Adding cores then does nothing.

Decision gravity. Lock granularity: one global lock (simple, no deadlocks, poor scaling), per-object locks (scales, deadlock risk), lock-free structures (best scaling, very hard to get right). Start coarse; refine only when profiling shows lock contention. It is reversible if the lock is hidden behind a small class; a one-way door if callers are expected to hold your lock.

Industry examples. The old Linux "Big Kernel Lock" (BKL) was one global lock; it took years (removed fully in 2.6.39) to split into fine-grained locks. CPython's GIL is the same trade: a single global lock makes the interpreter simple and single-thread fast but caps CPU-bound threads at about one core.

Everyday analogy. A single-stall toilet: everyone does other things in parallel, but only one person can be inside, and a long stay hurts everyone.

Common interview traps.

  • Doing I/O or calling unknown code (callbacks) while holding a lock: long hold times and hidden deadlocks.
  • Forgetting that reads need protection too if writers exist.
  • Not naming the three properties (exclusion, progress, bounded waiting).

notes.title: Mutex
notes.html:
A mutex (mutual exclusion lock) lets one thread own a critical section; others sleep until it is released. Operations: lock and unlock. The key point is that a waiting thread is put to sleep by the kernel, so it burns no CPU.

How Linux implements it (the futex, fast userspace mutex): the lock is one integer in user memory.

  • Uncontended lock: one atomic compare-and-swap from 0 to 1 in user space. No syscall. About 20 ns.
  • Contended lock: the thread calls the futex(FUTEX_WAIT) syscall and the kernel parks it. unlock sees waiters and calls futex(FUTEX_WAKE). A contended lock costs a syscall plus a context switch, about 2 to 10 microseconds.
# See it live: threads stuck on a mutex show as futex waits
strace -f -c -p 2310
# % time     seconds  usecs/call     calls    errors syscall
#  91.40    4.812211        1203      4000       812 futex
// Java: synchronized or ReentrantLock (both are mutexes with sleeping waiters)
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();
void withdraw(long amt) {
    lock.lock();
    try { if (balance >= amt) balance -= amt; }
    finally { lock.unlock(); }     // always unlock in finally
}

Properties to know: a mutex has an owner (only the locker may unlock). Recursive (reentrant) mutexes let the same thread lock again; Java synchronized and ReentrantLock are reentrant, a default pthread_mutex_t is not (relocking self-deadlocks). Priority inversion: a low-priority thread holds the lock, a high-priority one waits, a medium-priority thread keeps the CPU. The 1997 Mars Pathfinder kept resetting because of exactly this; the fix was enabling priority inheritance on the mutex (PTHREAD_PRIO_INHERIT).

Industry examples. Go's sync.Mutex has a normal mode and a "starvation mode" (after a waiter fails 1 ms, ownership is handed over directly). Java's synchronized starts as a cheap biased/thin lock and inflates to an OS-backed monitor under contention (biased locking was removed in JDK 18+).

Everyday analogy. A key to a single meeting room: take the key, use the room, hang the key back. If the key is gone you wait on the sofa (sleep), not by pounding on the door.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to unlock on an exception path. Use try/finally, RAII (std::lock_guard) or defer mu.Unlock().
  • Locking different locks for the same data in different code paths.
  • Thinking a mutex is free. Contended mutexes with many threads show up as futex time in strace and high context-switch rate in vmstat.

notes.title: Spinlock
notes.html:
A spinlock makes a waiting thread loop on the CPU until the lock frees, instead of sleeping. It wastes cycles while waiting but avoids the cost of a context switch, so it wins only when the lock is held for a very short time (less than the cost of sleeping, roughly under 1 to 2 microseconds).

Minimal test-and-set spinlock:

lock:    while (atomic_exchange(&flag, 1) == 1) { pause; }   // spin
unlock:  atomic_store(&flag, 0)

The pause (x86) hint reduces power and helps the sibling hyper-thread. Better variants: test-and-test-and-set (spin on a plain read first so the cache line stays shared, then try the atomic), and ticket / MCS locks (each waiter spins on its own cache line, fair and no cache-line stampede).

Worked example. Critical section = 100 ns. Sleeping and waking costs about 5 microseconds of latency. A spinner waits about 100 ns; a sleeper waits 5,000 ns, 50 times longer. But if the holder is preempted by the scheduler while holding the lock (on a single core, or oversubscribed), spinners burn their whole time slice (say 4 ms) doing nothing. Rule: spinlocks are for kernels and for short, non-preemptible sections.

Industry examples. The Linux kernel uses spinlocks everywhere in interrupt context, where sleeping is forbidden: the holder disables preemption (and often local interrupts) with spin_lock_irqsave. Queued spinlocks (qspinlock, MCS-based) are the modern kernel default. Many user-space libraries (glibc adaptive mutex, Java's adaptive spinning in monitors) spin briefly and then sleep: the best of both.

Everyday analogy. Waiting at a lift with the door about to open: you stand and stare for two seconds. If the lift is stuck on floor 30, you would walk away and read a book (sleep).

Common interview traps.

  • Using a pure spinlock in user space on an oversubscribed machine (more threads than cores). Throughput collapses.
  • Sleeping (calling anything that blocks, such as malloc with page fault or printk to a slow console) while holding a kernel spinlock: deadlock or "scheduling while atomic" panic.
  • Saying spinlocks are "faster". They are faster only for very short holds.

notes.title: Semaphores
notes.html:
A semaphore is a counter with two operations: wait (P, decrement, sleep if it would go below zero) and signal (V, increment, wake a sleeper). Dijkstra invented it in 1965. Unlike a mutex it has no owner: thread A can signal what thread B waited on.

Two main uses:

  • Counting semaphore (permits): initial value N means N resources. A connection pool of 20 is a semaphore starting at 20.
  • Binary semaphore (0/1) used as a signal: thread B waits, thread A signals "data is ready". This is how you order events across threads, which a mutex cannot do cleanly.
// Limit concurrent calls to a flaky downstream service to 10
private final Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(10);
String call() throws InterruptedException {
    permits.acquire();               // blocks if 10 are already in flight
    try { return http.get(url); }
    finally { permits.release(); }
}

Worked example. Downstream handles 200 concurrent requests before latency explodes. Each of your 8 app servers gets a semaphore of 25 (8 x 25 = 200). Excess callers either queue (bounded) or fail fast. This is the bulkhead pattern; Netflix Hystrix and Resilience4j implement it with semaphores or thread pools.

Linux has POSIX semaphores (sem_wait, sem_post, built on futexes) and System V semaphores (older, kernel objects, still seen in PostgreSQL's shared memory setup).

Decision gravity. Mutex vs binary semaphore: use a mutex for protecting data (ownership, priority inheritance, clear intent), a semaphore for counting resources or signalling. Reversible; mistakes show up as lost wake-ups or leaked permits.

Everyday analogy. A car park with 50 tickets: each car takes a ticket on entry and returns it on exit. At zero tickets the barrier stays shut.

Common interview traps.

  • Using a binary semaphore as a mutex and then releasing from the wrong place (no owner means no safety net).
  • Leaking permits on exceptions; always release in finally.
  • Not knowing semaphores can be initialised to 0 to mean "wait for an event".

notes.title: Condition variables
notes.html:
A condition variable lets a thread sleep until some condition on shared data becomes true. It always works together with a mutex that protects that data. Without it you either spin ("is it ready yet?") or sleep for a fixed time and waste latency.

Protocol (the pattern must be exactly this):

consumer:                          producer:
  lock(m)                            lock(m)
  while (queue is empty)             queue.push(item)
      wait(cv, m)   // atomically    signal(cv)
  item = queue.pop() // unlock+sleep unlock(m)
  unlock(m)

wait atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, then reacquires the mutex before returning. The while loop (not if) is mandatory for two reasons: spurious wake-ups (the OS may wake a waiter for no reason) and stolen wake-ups (another consumer got the item first between the signal and your reacquire).

final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();
Item take() throws InterruptedException {
    lock.lock();
    try {
        while (queue.isEmpty()) notEmpty.await();   // loop, not if
        return queue.poll();
    } finally { lock.unlock(); }
}

Signal vs broadcast. signal wakes one waiter, broadcast (notifyAll) wakes all. Use broadcast when waiters wait for different conditions on the same cv, or when unsure; it costs a "thundering herd" of wake-ups. Linux futex has FUTEX_REQUEUE so glibc can move waiters from the cv to the mutex without waking them all at once.

Industry examples. Java's BlockingQueue, Go's sync.Cond, Kotlin channels (under the hood coroutines park instead of sleeping a thread) are all this pattern. Android's Handler/Looper message queue blocks in epoll (native) until a message arrives.

Everyday analogy. A bakery pager: you leave your lock-box key at the counter, go to sit down, and the buzzer wakes you; you walk back, retake your place and check your order is actually there.

Common interview traps.

  • if instead of while around wait: the classic bug.
  • Signalling without holding the mutex or without changing the condition under it: a lost wake-up (signal fires before the waiter sleeps, nobody ever wakes it).
  • Using wait on a cv with a different mutex than the one protecting the state.

notes.title: Atomics
notes.html:
An atomic operation is a read-modify-write that the hardware guarantees cannot be interrupted or interleaved with other cores' accesses to that location. On x86 it uses the lock prefix (lock xadd, lock cmpxchg), which locks the cache line for the instruction. On ARM it uses load-linked/store-conditional pairs (ldaxr/stlxr) or newer LSE instructions.

Key operations: fetch_add, exchange, and compare-and-swap (CAS): "set to new only if currently equal to expected; tell me if it worked". CAS is the building block for lock-free code:

AtomicLong counter = new AtomicLong();
counter.incrementAndGet();                 // lock xadd, no mutex

// Lock-free "update max" using a CAS loop
void recordMax(AtomicLong max, long v) {
    long cur;
    while (v > (cur = max.get()) && !max.compareAndSet(cur, v)) { /* retry */ }
}

Worked example. 8 threads incrementing one counter 10 million times each. With a mutex: about 1.5 to 3 seconds (contention, sleeping). With an atomic: about 0.5 to 1 second, because all 8 cores fight for one cache line. With a sharded counter (each thread increments its own padded slot, sum on read): about 0.03 seconds. Java's LongAdder does exactly this. Atomics remove sleeping but not cache-line bouncing; at hot spots you must shard.

ABA problem. CAS checks only the value. Thread 1 reads A, is paused; thread 2 changes A to B and back to A (maybe a freed and reused node); thread 1's CAS succeeds although the structure changed. Fixes: version-tagged pointers (AtomicStampedReference), hazard pointers, epoch reclamation (RCU in the Linux kernel).

Decision gravity. Atomics are right for counters, flags, reference swaps. For multi-field invariants (balance and history together) use a lock; lock-free algorithms for those are research-grade bugs waiting to happen. Reversible if hidden behind a class.

Industry examples. Linux uses atomic_t and refcount_t for reference counts; Netty and Kafka clients use atomics and CAS for state flags; Disruptor (LMAX) built a lock-free ring buffer doing millions of messages/s per core.

Everyday analogy. Writing on a whiteboard with a rule: "erase 5 and write 6 only if it still says 5, otherwise look again". No one can sneak in a different number mid-edit.

Common interview traps.

  • "Lock-free is always faster." Under heavy contention a CAS loop can retry endlessly (it is lock-free, not wait-free).
  • Ignoring false sharing: two unrelated atomics on the same 64-byte cache line slow each other. Pad to separate lines.
  • Using two atomics and assuming the pair is consistent.

notes.title: Memory ordering and visibility
notes.html:
Modern CPUs and compilers reorder memory operations and cache them per core, so one thread may see another's writes late or in a different order. Single-threaded code never notices, because the result looks the same. Across threads it matters.

Why it happens: compilers move and cache variables in registers; CPUs have store buffers (a write sits in a queue before reaching the cache) and out-of-order execution. x86 is strong (TSO: only a store followed by a load to a different address may reorder). ARM and POWER are weak (almost any reordering allowed), which is why code that "works on x86" breaks on Android phones and Apple silicon servers.

The classic broken pattern:

shared: int data = 0; bool ready = false;
Thread A:  data = 42;  ready = true;
Thread B:  while (!ready) {}  print(data);   // may print 0, or loop forever

Fix: use release/acquire pairs. A release store makes all earlier writes visible before the flag; an acquire load that sees the flag sees those writes.

volatile boolean ready;   // Java volatile = acquire on read, release on write (sequentially consistent)
int data;
// Thread A: data = 42; ready = true;
// Thread B: while (!ready) {} ; use(data);   // guaranteed to see 42

C++/Rust give explicit orders: relaxed (atomicity only), acquire, release, acq_rel, seq_cst (global order, the default and the safest). A memory barrier/fence instruction (mfence, dmb) enforces ordering. Mutex lock is an acquire and unlock a release, so data protected by a mutex needs no extra fences. This is the "happens-before" relation in the Java Memory Model.

Worked example: double-checked locking. The old Java singleton if (inst == null) { synchronized { if (inst == null) inst = new Foo(); } } was broken before Java 5: the reference could be published before the constructor finished, so another thread used a half-built object. Fix: declare inst volatile.

Decision gravity. Use seq_cst/volatile/mutexes by default. Weaker orderings give a few percent on hot paths and cost days of reasoning; choose them only with a benchmark and a tool such as ThreadSanitizer or a model checker (CDSChecker, Loom for Rust). Reversible at code level, but wrong code ships silently.

Industry examples. Linux kernel has a formal memory model (smp_mb(), READ_ONCE, WRITE_ONCE, smp_store_release). Java JMM (JSR-133, 2004) fixed volatile semantics. Go's memory model says a channel send happens before the matching receive completes.

Everyday analogy. Two colleagues each keep a private notebook copy of a shared plan and sync only now and then; without a "sync point" one may act on an old page.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying volatile in C/C++ gives thread safety. It does not (it only stops some compiler optimisations). Use std::atomic.
  • Assuming x86 behaviour proves correctness on ARM.
  • Forgetting that a plain boolean stop flag may never be seen as changed (the JIT can hoist the read out of the loop).

notes.title: Choosing a primitive and finding contention in production
notes.html:
Pick the simplest primitive that is correct, then measure. A decision ladder:

Need Use
Protect a multi-field invariant Mutex
Wait until a condition holds Mutex plus condition variable (or a blocking queue)
Limit N concurrent users of a resource Semaphore
Counter, flag, single pointer swap Atomic
Tiny critical section in a kernel or interrupt Spinlock
Many readers, rare writers Reader-writer lock, or copy-on-write / RCU
Avoid sharing altogether Message passing, thread confinement, per-thread data

Spotting lock contention on a live Linux box:

$ vmstat 1 3
procs -----------memory---------- ---swap-- -----io---- -system-- ------cpu-----
 r  b   swpd   free   buff  cache   si   so    bi    bo   in   cs us sy id wa st
12  0      0 812304 120044 2210032    0    0     0     4 9120 118000 38 22 40  0  0

A high cs (context switches, here 118k/s) with CPU idle (id 40) while the app is slow hints at threads parking on locks. Confirm per thread:

pidstat -w -t -p 2310 1      # voluntary context switches per thread
perf trace -s -p 2310 -- sleep 5   # futex dominates the syscall summary
jstack 2310 | grep -A3 "BLOCKED"   # Java: who waits for which monitor

Industry examples. Instagram and Dropbox have both published Python/Go services that stalled on a hot lock around a shared cache; the fix was sharding the lock (hash key to one of 64 locks), the standard first step. Java ConcurrentHashMap does lock striping (bins) by design.

Everyday analogy. Traffic: first remove the shared road (separate lanes), then add a signal (lock) only where roads must cross.

Common interview traps.

  • Optimising with lock-free code before measuring contention.
  • Using a read-write lock where writes are frequent: it is slower than a plain mutex because of bookkeeping and writer starvation rules.
  • Not mentioning lock ordering and keeping critical sections short as the first cures.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• A race condition is timing-dependent wrongness; counter++ is load, add, store. Detect with ThreadSanitizer or Go -race.
  • Keep critical sections tiny; Amdahl's law says the serial part caps speed-up.
  • Mutex: sleeping lock built on futex (fast path in user space, slow path syscall). Release on all paths; beware priority inversion.
  • Spinlock: busy-wait, only for very short holds, mostly kernel and interrupt context.
  • Semaphore: a counter for N resources or for signalling; no owner.
  • Condition variable: always with a mutex and a while loop; handles spurious and stolen wake-ups.
  • Atomics and CAS: lock-free building blocks; watch ABA, contention and false sharing; shard hot counters.
  • Memory ordering: caches, store buffers and compilers reorder; use release/acquire, volatile (Java) or std::atomic; mutexes already give the fences.
  • In production: high context switches plus idle CPU plus futex in strace points to lock contention.
